chunks: "Impedance is square root of L over C per unit length, so I change geometry to change that ratio.
The layout knob is trace width: wider means more capacitance to the plane, so lower impedance; narrower raises it.
The biggest physical knob is the dielectric height between trace and plane: thicker dielectric means less capacitance and a higher impedance, thinner means lower.

Dielectric constant works the other way: higher epsilon means more capacitance and lower impedance, which is why RF boards use lower-epsilon laminates and end up with wider traces for the same 50 ohms.
Smaller effects: thicker copper behaves a bit like a wider trace, so impedance drops slightly, and solder mask over microstrip lowers it by a couple of ohms.
Putting coplanar ground pour beside the trace lowers impedance, which is how coplanar waveguide is tuned by the gap.
For a differential pair, spacing matters too: closer coupling lowers the differential impedance. For numbers: on 0. 2 mm FR-4 with 1 oz copper, a 0. 36 mm trace is 50 ohms.
Ten percent wider drops it about 2. 6 ohms; ten percent more dielectric height raises it by about 2. 9 ohms.
In practice I choose the stackup with the fab, then set the width with their field solver."
